entries.de95d5fe213e92e59ad826cc671a1a1fddbe9368: <div eID="gen19543" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19544" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19545" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19545" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19544" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19546" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, with strong confidence in God, in a time of distress prays earnestly for deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.1-Psa.31.5">Psa 31:1-5</reference>. He expresses his abhorrence of evil, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.6">Psa 31:6</reference>; gratefully mentions former interpositions of God, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.7">Psa 31:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference>; continues to detail the miseries of his case, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.9-Psa.31.18">Psa 31:9-18</reference>; points out the privileges of them that fear God, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; shows that God had heard his prayers, notwithstanding he had given himself over for lost, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.21">Psa 31:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>; calls on the saints to love God, and to have confidence in him, because he preserves the faithful, and plentifully rewards the proud doer, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.31.24">Psa 31:24</reference>. <div eID="gen19546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19547" type="x-p"/> This Psalm contains no notes of time or place, to help us to ascertain when, where, or on what account it was written. Nor have we any certain evidence relative to the author: it might have been written by David during his persecution by Saul. Some think Jeremiah to have been the author: the thirteenth verse begins exactly with the same words as <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>. There are several other apparent references to passages in the book of Jeremiah, which shall be produced in the notes. <div eID="gen19547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19548" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19549" type="x-p"/> In thee, O Lord, do I put my trust - I confide in thee for every good I need: let me not be confounded by not receiving the end of my faith, the supply of my wants, and the salvation of my soul.
entries.458cb03a105bbb4a178b604d7760c90fe2935fd2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19550" type="x-p"/> Bow down thine ear - Listen to my complaint. Put thy ear to my lips, that thou mayest hear all that my feebleness is capable of uttering. We generally put our ear near to the lips of the sick and dying, that we may hear what they say. To this the text appears to allude. <div eID="gen19550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19551" type="x-p"/> Strong rock - Rocks, rocky places, or caves in the rocks, were often strong places in the land of Judea. To such natural fortifications allusions are repeatedly made by the Hebrew poetic writers.
entries.523662d56d2a9adbc4428e86b9ab85e205297ed8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19552" type="x-p"/> Pull me out of the net - They have hemmed me in on every side, and I cannot escape but by miracle.
entries.14218532d97f595fd8f773b58608ebab5b1b91bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19553" type="x-p"/> Into thine hand I commit my spirit - These words, as they stand in the Vulgate, were in the highest credit among our ancestors; by whom they were used in all dangers, difficulties, and in the article of death. In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum, was used by the sick when about to expire, if they were sensible; and if not, the priest said it in their behalf. In forms of prayer for sick and dying persons, these words were frequently inserted in Latin, though all the rest of the prayer was English; for it was supposed there was something sovereign in the language itself. But let not the abuse of such words hinder their usefullness. For an ejaculation nothing can be better; and when the pious or the tempted with confidence use them, nothing can exceed their effect. "Into thy hands I commend my spirit; for thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth." I give my soul to thee, for it is thine: thou hast redeemed it by thy blood; it is safe nowhere but in thy hand. Thou hast promised to save them that trust in thee; thou art the God of truth, and canst not deny thyself. But these words are particularly sanctified, or set apart for this purpose, by the use made of them by our blessed Lord just before he expired on the cross. "And when Jesus had cried with a loud voice, he said, Πατερ, εις χειρας σου παρατιθεμαι το πνευμα μου· 'Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit,'" <reference osisRef="Luk.23.46">Luk 23:46</reference>. The rest of the verse was not suitable to the Savior of the world, and therefore he omits it; but it is suitable to us who have been redeemed by that sacrificial death. St. Stephen uses nearly the same words, and they were the last that he uttered. <reference osisRef="Act.7.59">Act 7:59</reference>.
entries.75313fafe2be99e584d3d639a6938a2ee940eb43: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19554" type="x-p"/> I have hated them - That is, I have abominated their ways. Idolaters are the persons of whom David speaks. <div eID="gen19554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19555" type="x-p"/> I trust in the Lord - While they trust in vanities vain things; (for an idol is nothing in the worid); and in lying vanities; (for much is promised and nothing given); I trust in Jehovah, who is God all-sufficient, and is my Shepherd, and therefore I shall lack no good thing.
entries.64a9c2a97bcd4a5ce8e70ce0e78f51ef36940efb: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19556" type="x-p"/> Thou hast known my soul in adversities - When all forsook me; when none could help me; when I could not save my own life; when my enemies were sure that I could not escape; then I found thee to be my Friend and Supporter. When friend, so called, finds it convenient not to know his friend in affliction and poverty, then thou didst acknowledge me as thine own, all worthless as I was. Human friendships may fail; but the Friend of sinners never fails. Cicero defines a real friend, Amicus certus in re incerta cernitor: "A friend in need is a friend indeed." Reader, such a Friend is the Lord.
entries.8dbf5651d1a2c51450650e84a74e172ec108e8cf: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19557" type="x-p"/> Thou hast set my foot in a large room - Many hair-breadth escapes David had for his life; at that time especially when, playing before Saul, the furious king took a spear and endeavored to pierce him through the body, but he escaped and got to the deserts. Here God, who had saved his life, set his feet in a large room. The seventh and eighth verses speak of what God had done previously for him.
entries.5c8a0df01cef1d69f8d9b71e7947ced853bc6c2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19558" type="x-p"/> Mine eye is consumed - He now returns, and speaks of his present situation. Grief had brought many tears from his eyes, many agonies into his soul, and many distressful feelings into his whole frame. <div eID="gen19558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19559" type="x-p"/> My soul and my belly - The belly is often taken for the whole body. But the term belly or bowels, in such as case as this, may be the most proper; for in distress and misery, the bowels being the most tender part, and in fact the very seat of compassion, they are often most affected. In Greek the word σπλαγχνον signifies a bowel, and σπλαγχνιζομαι signifies to be moved with compassion; to feel misery in the bowels at the sight of a person in pain and distress.
entries.3d706969b62ff5030f7e6c120fe88cbeb651726f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19560" type="x-p"/> My life is spent with grief - My life is a life of suffering and distress, and by grief my days are shortened. Grief disturbs the functions of life, prevents the due concoction of food, injures the digestive organs, destroys appetite, impairs the nervous system, relaxes the muscles, induces morbid action in the animal economy, and hastens death. These effects are well expressed in the verse itself. <div eID="gen19560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19561" type="x-p"/> My years with sighing - אנחה anachah. This is a mere natural expression of grief; the very sounds which proceed from a distressed mind; an-ach-ah! common, with little variation, to all nations, and nearly the same in all languages. The och-och-on of the Irish is precisely the same sound, and the same sense. Thousands of beauties or this kind are to be found in the sacred language.
entries.c91db0296357d674598fc17f7db5a6e29e6f9691: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19562" type="x-p"/> I was a reproach - When proscribed at the court of Saul, my enemies triumphed, and loaded me with execrations; my neighbors considered me as a dangerous man, now deservedlJr driven from society; my acquaintance, who knew me best, were afraid to hold any communication with me; and they who saw me in my exile avoided me as if affected with a contagious disorder,
entries.59ede538411b94a30090a0b076a5a38ee1f489ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen19562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19563" type="x-p"/> I am forgotten as a dead man - I am considered as a person adjudged to death. I am like a broken vessel-like a thing totally useless.
entries.dd224e5cef17adf1d8c28ecfbbe17e3400948b67: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen19563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19564" type="x-p"/> I have heard the slander of many - To this and the two foregoing verses the reader may find several parallels; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer 18:18</reference> to the end of <reference osisRef="Jer.19.1-Jer.19.15">Jer 19:1-15</reference>., and ten first verses of chapter 20: This has caused several to suppose that Jeremiah was the author of this Psalm.
entries.1c1b368175dd2251c8523e97d52dbb1e18f4f4aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen19564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19565" type="x-p"/> But I trusted in thee - Hitherto thou hast been my Helper, and thou art my God; I have taken thee for my eternal portion.
entries.c1663eb605c61fb7cde424e0a0691646e375c55d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen19565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19566" type="x-p"/> My times are in thy hand - The events of my life are under thy control. No danger can happen to me without thy foresight; thou seest what is prepared for or meditated against me; thou canst therefore deliver me from mine enemies.
entries.05945b544990fda8c5e2284c2867b2e790b940aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen19566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19567" type="x-p"/> Make thy face to shine upon thy servant - Only let me know that thou art reconciled to and pleased with me, and then, come what will, all must be well. <div eID="gen19567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19568" type="x-p"/> Save me for thy mercies' sake - Literally, Save me in thy mercy.
entries.79f1730a090721bc7ffed227d3697e470eb7862d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen19568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19569" type="x-p"/> Let the wicked be ashamed - Those who traduce my character and lay snares for my life; let them be confounded.
entries.c7dc0887b9432ef110dd7c23f1991e407848619e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen19569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19570" type="x-p"/> Let the lying lips be put to silence - As to my enemies, persecutors, and slanderers, abate their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices. See <reference osisRef="Jer.18.18">Jer 18:18</reference>.
entries.ef87d9d2eae2a0a6072704328fe0f1e6af034f1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen19570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19571" type="x-p"/> O how great is thy goodness - God's goodness is infinite; there is enough for all. enough for each, enough for evermore. It is laid up where neither devils nor men can reach it, and it is laid up for them that fear the Lord; therefore every one who trembles at his word, may expect all he needs from this Fountain that can never be dried ufp. <div eID="gen19571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19572" type="x-p"/> Which thou hast wrought - Thou hast already prepared it; it is the work of thy own hands; thou hast provided it and proportioned it to the necessities of men, and all who trust in thee shall have it. And for them especially it is prepared who trust in thee before men - who boldly confess thee amidst a crooked and perverse generation.
entries.02f3dabd1ba26db0b25eba15d4f2faa28ef432d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen19572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19573" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence - בסתר פניך besether paneycha, "With the covering of thy countenance." Their life shall be so hidden with Christ in God, that their enemies shall not be able to find them out. To such a hiding-place Satan himself dare not approach. There the pride of man cannot come. <div eID="gen19573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19574" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion - Thou shalt put them in the innermost part of thy tent. This implies that they shall have much communion and union with God; that they shall be transformed into his likeness, and have his highest approbation.
entries.841b3d763aecac9879c655be76015ac9ff0b2a25: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen19574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19575" type="x-p"/> In a strong city - If this Psalm was written by David, this must refer to his taking refuge with achish, king of Gath, who gave him Ziklag, a fortified city, to secure himself and followers in. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sam 27:6</reference>. This is more likely than that it was Keilah, where he only had intimation of the traitorous design of the inhabitants to deliver him up to Saul; so that the place was no refuge to him, howsoever fortified. Perhaps the passage may mean that, under the protection of God, he was as safe as if he had been in a fortified city.
entries.a5f59a0a75ad9f77c89c169f1b229f8516d3367d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen19575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19576" type="x-p"/> I said in my haste - Not duly adverting to the promise of God, I was led to conclude that my enemies were so strong, so numerous, and had so many advantages against me, that I must necessarily fall into and by their hands; however, I continued to pray, and thou didst hear the voice of my supplication.
entries.1832f0bb2a1bb481b9843cdcf2e94df23b06612a: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen19576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19577" type="x-p"/> O love the Lord, all ye his saints - It is only the saints that can love God, as they only are made partakers of the Divine nature. Holy spirits can love God, who is the fountain of their holiness; and the saints should love him. <div eID="gen19577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19578" type="x-p"/> Preserveth the faithful - Those who, being filled with the love of God, bring forth the fruits of that love - universal obedience to the will of God; for to such persons his commands are not grievous, their duty is their delight; while a man is faithful to the grace he has received, that is, uses and improves the talents with which God has intrusted him, God's service is perfect freedom. <div eID="gen19578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19579" type="x-p"/> The proud doer - The man of the proud heart, haughty and supercilious carriage, and insulting and outrageous conduct. A proud man is peculiarly odious in the sight of God; and in the sight of reason how absurd! A sinner, a fallen spirit, an heir of wretchedness and corruption-proud! <div eID="gen19579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19580" type="x-p"/> Proud of what? Of an indwelling devil! Well; such persons shall be plentifully rewarded. They shall get their due, their whole due, and nothing but their due.
entries.3aba23dfbfe325a215bda8f23c0e84e5fb8632d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen19580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19581" type="x-p"/> Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart - In <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">1Cor 16:13</reference>, St. Paul says, "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith; quit you like men; be strong:" Γρηγορειτε, στηκετε εν τῃ πιστει, ανδριζεσθε, κραταιουσθε. The latter words he seems to have borrowed from the Septuagint, who translate, "Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart," by Ανδριζεσθε και κραταιουσθω ἡ καρδια ὑμων "Act like men, and your hearts shall be strengthened." They that hope in God, and are endeavoring to walk carefully before him, may take courage at all times, and expect the fullness of the blessing of the Gospel of peace.  <chapter eID="Ps.31"/> <div eID="gen19581" type="x-p"/>

entries.5d4b22f3ab3389085a63715e21d7ca72de8c1a6f: <div eID="gen9358" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Surrender of One Sorely Persecuted into the Hand of God</title> <div sID="gen9359" type="x-p"/> In Ps 31 the poet also, in ואני אמרתּי (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>), looks back upon a previous state of mind, viz., that of conflict, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Psa 30:7</reference> upon that of security. And here, also, he makes all the חסידים partakers with him of the healthful fruit of his deliverance (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.31.24">Psa 31:24</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Psa 30:5</reference>). But in other respects the situation of the two Psalms is very different. They are both Davidic. Hitzig, however, regards them both as composed by Jeremiah. With reference to Ps 31, which Ewald also ascribes to “Jéremjá,” this view is well worthy of notice. Not only do we find <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.14">Psa 31:14</reference></hi> recurring in Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>, but the whole Psalm, in its language (cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lam.1.20">Lam 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.11">Psa 31:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.20.18">Jer 20:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.18">Psa 31:18</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">Jer 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference> with <reference osisRef="Lam.3.54">Lam 3:54</reference>) and its plaintive tenderness, reminds one of Jeremiah. But this relationship does not decide the question. The passage <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>, like many other passages of this prophet, whose language is so strongly imbued with that of the Psalter, may be just as much a reminiscence as <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">Jon 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:9</reference>; and as regards its plaintive tenderness there are no two characters more closely allied naturally and in spirit than David and Jeremiah; both are servants of Jahve, whose noble, tender spirits were capable of strong feeling, who cherished earnest longings, and abounded in tribulations. We abide, though not without some degree of hesitation, by the testimony of the inscription; and regard the Psalm as a song springing from the outward and inward conflict (lxx ἐκστάσεως, probably by a combination of <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>, ἐν ἐκστάσει, בחפזי, with <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26">1Sa 23:26</reference>) of the time of Saul. While <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference></hi> is not suited to the mouth of the captive Jeremiah (Hitzig), the Psalm has much that is common not only to Ps 69 (more especially <reference osisRef="Ps.69.9">Psa 69:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.33">Psa 69:33</reference>), a Psalm that sounds much like Jeremiah’s, but also to others, which we regard as Davidic; viz., the figures corresponding to the life of warfare which David then lived among the rocks and caves of the wilderness; the cheering call, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.25">Jer 31:25</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.22.27">Psa 22:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">Psa 27:14</reference>; the rare use of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. הפליא <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.7">Psa 17:7</reference>; the desire to be hidden by God, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.21">Psa 31:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.3">Psa 64:3</reference>; etc. In common with Ps 22 this may be noted, that the crucified Christ takes His last word from this Psalm, just as He takes His last utterance but three from that Psalm. But in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.10-Ps.31.14">Psa 31:10-14</reference>, the prefigurement of the Passion is confined within the limits of the type and does not undergo the same prophetical enhancement as it does in that unique Ps 22, to which only Ps 69 is in any degree comparable. The opening, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>, is repeated in the centonic Ps 71, the work of a later anonymous poet, just as <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference> is in part repeated in Psa 116:11. The arrangement of the strophes is not very clear.
entries.2e5cf7680f6a506ae789c4954543810eb8fd5f35: <reference osisRef="Ps.31.1-Ps.31.8">Psa 31:1-8</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_31:2-9) The poet begins with the prayer for deliverance, based upon the trust which Jahve, to whom he surrenders himself, cannot possibly disappoint; and rejoices beforehand in the protection which he assumes will, without any doubt, be granted. Out of his confident security in God (הסיתי) springs the prayer: may it never come to this with me, that I am put to confusion by the disappointment of my hope. This prayer in the form of intense desire is followed by prayers in the direct form of supplication. The supplicatory פלּטני is based upon God’s righteousness, which cannot refrain from repaying conduct consistent with the order of redemption, though after prolonged trial, with the longed for tokens of deliverance. In the second paragraph, the prayer is moulded in accordance with the circumstances of him who is chased by Saul hither and thither among the mountains and in the desert, homeless and defenceless. In the expression צוּר מעוז, מעוז is <hi type="italic">genit. appositionis:</hi> a rock of defence (מעוז from עזז, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1">Psa 27:1</reference>), or rather: of refuge (מעוז = Arab. <hi type="italic">m‛âd</hi>, from עוּז, עוז = Arab. <hi type="italic">'âd</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.39">Psa 37:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.9">Psa 52:9</reference>, and probably also in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Isa 30:2</reference> and elsewhere);<note placement="foot">It can hardly be doubted, that, in opposition to the pointing as we have it, which only recognises one מעוז (מעז) from עזז, to be strong, there are two different substantives having this principal form, viz., מעז a fortress, secure place, bulwark, which according to its derivation is inflected מעזּי, etc., and מעוז equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">ma‛âdh</hi>, a hiding-place, defence, refuge, which ought to have been declined מעוזי or מעוּזי like the synonymous מנוּסי (Olshausen §201, 202). Moreover עוּז, Arab. <hi type="italic">'âd</hi>, like חסה, of which it is the parallel word in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Isa 30:2</reference>, means to hide one’s self anywhere (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., Hebrew העיז, according to the Kamus, Zamachshari and Neshwân: to hide any one, e.g., Koran 3:31); hence Arab. <hi type="italic">'â‛d</hi>, a plant that grows among bushes (<hi type="italic">bên esh - shôk</hi> according to the Kamus) or in the crevices of the rocks (<hi type="italic">fi-l-hazn</hi> according to Neshwân) and is thus inaccessible to the herds; Arab. <hi type="italic">'wwad</hi>, gazelles that are invisible, i.e., keep hidden, for seven days after giving birth, also used of pieces of flesh of which part is hidden among the bones; Arab. <hi type="italic">'ûdat</hi>, an amulet with which a man covers himself (<hi type="italic">protegit</hi></note>, and so forth. - Wetzstein. <div eID="gen9359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9360" type="x-p"/> Consequently מעוז (formed like Arab. <hi type="italic">m‛âd</hi>, according to Neshwân equivalent to Arab<hi type="italic">. ma'wad</hi>) is prop. a place in which to hide one’s self, synonymous with מחסה, מנוס, Arab. <hi type="italic">mlâd , malja‛</hi>, and the like. True, the two substantives from עזז and עוז meet in their meanings like <hi type="italic">praesidium</hi> and <hi type="italic">asylum</hi>, and according to passages like <reference osisRef="Jer.16.19">Jer 16:19</reference> appear to be blended in the genius of the language, but they are radically distinct.) a rock-castle, i.e., a castle upon a rock, would be called מעוז צוּר, reversing the order of the words. צוּר מעוז in <reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">Psa 71:3</reference>, a rock of habitation, i.e., of safe sojourn, fully warrants this interpretation. מצוּדה, prop. <hi type="italic">specula</hi>, signifies a mountain height or the summit of a mountain; a house on the mountain height is one that is situated on some high mountain top and affords a safe asylum (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>). The thought “show me Thy salvation, for Thou art my Saviour,” underlies the connection expressed by כּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.4">Psa 31:4</reference> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference></hi>. Löster considers it to be illogical, but it is the logic of every believing prayer. The poet prays that God would become to him, <hi type="italic">actu reflexo</hi>, that which to the <hi type="italic">actus directus</hi> of his faith He is even now. The futures in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.4">Psa 31:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference> express hopes which necessarily arise out of that which Jahve is to the poet. The interchangeable notions הנחה and נהל, with which we are familiar from <reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference>, stand side by side, in order to give urgency to the utterance of the longing for God’s gentle and safe guidance. Instead of translating it “out of the net, which etc.,” according to the accents (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.8">Psa 12:8</reference>) it should be rendered “out of the net there,” so that טמנוּ לּי is a relative clause without the relative. <div eID="gen9360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9361" type="x-p"/> Into the hand of this God, who is and will be all this to him, he commends his spirit; he gives it over into His hand as a trust or deposit (פּקּדון); for whatsoever is deposited there is safely kept, and freed from all danger and all distress. The word used is not נפשׁי, which Theodotion substitutes when he renders it τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ψυχὴν τῇ σῇ παρατίθημι προμηθείᾳ but רוּחי; and this is used designedly. The language of the prayer lays hold of life at its root, as springing directly from God and as also living in the believer from God and in God; and this life it places under His protection, who is the true life of all spirit-life (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.16">Isa 38:16</reference>) and of all life. It is the language of prayer with which the dying Christ breathed forth His life, Luk 23:46. The period of David’s persecution by Saul is the most prolific in types of the Passion; and this language of prayer, which proceeded from the furnace of affliction through which David at that time passed, denotes, in the mouth of Christ a crisis in the history of redemption in which the Old Testament receives its fulfilment. Like David, He commends His spirit to God; but not, that He may not die, but that dying He may not die, i.e., that He may receive back again His spirit-corporeal life, which is hidden in the hand of God, in imperishable power and glory. That which is so ardently desired and hoped for is regarded by him, who thus in faith commends himself to God, as having already taken place, “Thou hast redeemed me, Jahve, God of truth.” The perfect פּדיתה is not used here, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference>, of that which is past, but of that which is already as good as past; it is not precative (Ew. §223, <hi type="italic">b</hi>), but, like the perfects in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.9">Psa 31:9</reference>, an expression of believing anticipation of redemption. It is the <hi type="italic">praet. confidentiae</hi> which is closely related to the <hi type="italic">praet. prophet</hi>.; for the spirit of faith, like the spirit of the prophets, speaks of the future with historic certainty. In the notion of אל אמת it is impossible to exclude the reference to false gods which is contained in אלהי אמת, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference>, since, in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Psa 31:7</reference>, “vain illusions” are used as an antithesis. הבלים, ever since <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">Deu 32:21</reference>, has become a favourite name for idols, and more particularly in Jeremiah (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.8.1-Ps.9.19">Psa 8:1-9 :19</reference>). On the other hand, according to the context, it may also not differ very greatly from אל אמוּנה, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deu 32:4</reference>; since the idea of God as a depositary or trustee still influences the thought, and אמת and אמוּנה are used interchangeably in other passages as personal attributes. We may say that אמת is being that lasts and verifies itself, and אמונה is sentiment that lasts and verifies itself. Therefore אל אמת is the God, who as the true God, maintains the truth of His revelation, and more especially of His promises, by a living authority or rule. <div eID="gen9361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Psa 31:7</reference>, David appeals to his entire and simple surrender to this true and faithful God: hateful to him are those, who worship vain images, whilst he, on the other hand, cleaves to Jahve. It is the false gods, which are called הבלי־שׁוא, as beings without being, which are of no service to their worshippers and only disappoint their expectations. Probably (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.6">Psa 5:6</reference>) it is to be read שׂנאת with the lxx, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic versions (Hitzig, Ewald, Olshausen, and others). In the text before us, which gives us no corrective <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.21">2Sa 14:21</reference>; Rth 4:5, ואני is not an antithesis to the preceding clause, but to the member of that clause which immediately precedes it. In Jonah’s psalm, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>, this is expressed by משׁמּרים הבלי־שׁוא; in the present instance the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> is used in the signification <hi type="italic">observare, colere</hi>, as in Hos 4:10, and even in Pro 27:18. In the waiting of service is included, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.59.10">Psa 59:10</reference>, the waiting of trust. The word בּטח which denotes the <hi type="italic">fiducia fidei</hi> is usually construed with בּ of adhering to, or על of resting upon; but here it is combined with אל of hanging on. The cohortatives in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.8">Psa 31:8</reference> express intentions. Olshausen and Hitzig translate them as optatives: may I be able to rejoice; but this, as a continuation of <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Psa 31:7</reference>, seems less appropriate. Certain that he will be heard, he determines to manifest thankful joy for Jahve’s mercy, that (אשׁר as in <reference osisRef="Gen.34.27">Gen 34:27</reference>) He has regarded (ἐπέβλεψε, <reference osisRef="Luke.1.48">Luk 1:48</reference>) his affliction, that He has known and exerted Himself about his soul’s distresses. The construction ידע בּ, in the presence of <reference osisRef="Gen.19.33">Gen 19:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.35">Gen 19:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.9">Job 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>, cannot be doubted (Hupfeld); it is more significant than the expression “to know of anything;” בּ is like ἐπὶ in ἐπιγιγνώσκειν used of the perception or comprehensive knowledge, which grasps an object and takes possession of it, or makes itself master of it. הסגּיר, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.9">Psa 31:9</reference>, συγκλείειν, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.11">1Sa 23:11</reference> (in the mouth of David) is so to abandon, that the hand of another closes upon that which is abandoned to it, i.e., has it completely in its power. מרחב, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">Psa 18:20</reference>, cf. Psa 26:12. The language is David’s, in which the language of the Tôra, and more especially of Deuteronomy (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.30">Deu 32:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.16">Deu 23:16</reference>), is re-echoed.
entries.5e5fee12f1368af18536c6be50a8d34312636476: <reference osisRef="Ps.31.9-Ps.31.13">Psa 31:9-13</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_31:10-14) After the paean before victory, which he has sung in the fulness of his faith, in this second part of the Psalm (with groups, or strophes, of diminishing compass: 6. 5. 4) there again breaks forth the petition, based upon the greatness of the suffering which the psalmist, after having strengthened himself in his trust in God, now all the more vividly sets before Him. צר־לּי, <hi type="italic">angustum est mihi</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.18">Psa 69:18</reference>, cf. Psa 18:7. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.10">Psa 31:10</reference></hi> is word for word like <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference>, except that in this passage to עיני, the eye which mirrors the state of suffering in which the sensuous perception and objective receptivity of the man are concentrated, are added נפשׁ, the soul forming the <hi type="italic">nexus</hi> of the spirit and the body, and בּטן, the inward parts of the body reflecting the energies and feelings of the spirit and the soul. חיּים, with which is combined the idea of the organic intermingling of the powers of soul and body, has the predicate in the plural, as in Psa 88:4. The fact that the poet makes mention of his iniquity as that by which his physical strength has become tottering (כּשׁל as in <reference osisRef="Neh.4.4">Neh 4:4</reference>), is nothing surprising even in a Psalm that belongs to the time of his persecution by Saul; for the longer this persecution continued, the more deeply must David have felt that he needed this furnace of affliction. <div eID="gen9362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> The text of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.12">Psa 31:12</reference></hi> upon which the lxx rendering is based, was just the same as ours: παρὰ πάντας τοὺς ἐχθρούς μου ἐγενήθην ὄνειδος καὶ τοῖς γείτοσί μου σφόδρα καὶ φόβος τοῖς γνωστοῖς μου. But this σφδόρα (Jerome <hi type="italic">nimis</hi>) would certainly only be tolerable, if it could be rendered, “I am become a reproach even to my neighbours exceedingly” - in favour of this position of מאד we might compare Jdg 12:2, - and this rendering is not really an impossible one; for not only has ו frequently the sense of “even” as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.23">2Sa 1:23</reference>, but (independently of passages, in which it may even be explained as “and that,” an expression which takes up what has been omitted, as in <reference osisRef="Amos.4.10">Amo 4:10</reference>) it sometimes has this meaning direct (like καὶ, <hi type="italic">et</hi> -<hi type="italic">etiam</hi>), <reference osisRef="Isa.32.7">Isa 32:7</reference>; Hos 8:6 (according to the accents), <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.5">2Ch 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.5">Ecc 5:5</reference> (cf. Ew. §352, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). Inasmuch, however, as this usage, in Hebrew, was not definitely developed, but was only as it were just developing, it may be asked whether it is not possible to find a suitable explanation without having recourse to this rendering of the ו as equivalent to גּם, a rendering which is always hazardous. Olshausen places ולשׁכני after למידעי, a change which certainly gets rid of all difficulty. Hitzig alters מאד into מנּד, frightened, scared. But one naturally looks for a parallel substantive to חרפּה, somewhat like “terror” (Syriac) or “burden.” Still מגור (dread) and משּׂאת (a burden) do not look as though מאד could be a corruption of either of those words. Is it not perhaps possible for מאד itself to be equivalent in meaning to משׂאת? Since in the signification σφόδρα it is so unsuited to this passage, the expression would not be ambiguous, if it were here used in a special sense. J. D. Michaelis has even compared the Arabic <hi type="italic">awd</hi>(<hi type="italic">awdat</hi>) in the sense of <hi type="italic">onus</hi>. We can, without the hesitation felt by Maurer and Hupfeld, suppose that מאד has indeed this meaning in this passage, and without any necessity for its being pointed מאד; for even the adverb מאד is originally a substantive derived from אוּד, Arab. <hi type="italic">âd</hi> (after the form מצד from צוּד) <hi type="italic">gravitas, firmitas</hi>, which is then used in the sense of <hi type="italic">graviter, firmiter</hi> (cf. the French <hi type="italic">ferme</hi>). אוּד, Arab. <hi type="italic">âd</hi>, however, has the radical signification to be compressed, compact, firm, and solid, from which proceed the significations, which are divided between <hi type="italic">âda , jaı̂du</hi>, and <hi type="italic">âda , jaûdu</hi>, to be strong, powerful, and to press upon, to burden, both of which meanings Arab. <hi type="italic">'dd</hi> unites within itself (cf. on <reference osisRef="Ps.20.9">Psa 20:9</reference>). <div eID="gen9363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9364" type="x-p"/> The number of opponents that David had, at length made him a reproach even in the eyes of the better disposed of his people, as being a revolter and usurper. Those among whom he found friendly shelter began to feel themselves burdened by his presence because they were thereby imperilled; and we see from the sad fate of Abimelech and the other priests of Nob what cause, humanly speaking, they, who were not merely slightly, but even intimately acquainted with him (מידּעים as inn <reference osisRef="Ps.55.14">Psa 55:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.9">Psa 88:9</reference>, 19), had for avoiding all intercourse with him. Thus, then, he is like one dead, whom as soon as he is borne out of his home to the grave, men are wont, in general, to put out of mind also (נשׁכּח מלּא, <hi type="italic">oblivione extingui ex corde</hi>; cf. מפּה, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.21">Deu 31:21</reference>). All intimate connection with him is as it were sundered, he is become כּכלי אבד, - a phrase, which, as we consider the confirmation which follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.14">Psa 31:14</reference>, has the sense of <hi type="italic">vas periens</hi> (not <hi type="italic">vas perditum</hi>), a vessel that is in the act of אבד, i.e., one that is set aside or thrown away, being abandoned to utter destruction and no more cared for (cf. Hos 8:8, together with <reference osisRef="Jer.48.38">Jer 48:38</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jer 22:28</reference>). With כּי he gives the ground for his comparison of himself to a household vessel that has become worthless. The insinuations and slanders of many brand him as a transgressor, dread surrounds him on every side (this is word for word the same as in <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>, where the prophet, with whom in other passages also מגור מסּביב is a frequent and standing formula, under similar circumstances uses the language of the psalmist); when they come together to take counsel concerning him (according to the accents the second half of the verse begins with בּהוּסדם), they think only how they may get rid of him. If the construction of ב with its infinitive were intended to be continued in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.14">Psa 31:14</reference></hi>, it would have been וזממוּ לקחת נפשׁי or לקחת נפשׁי יזמּוּ.
entries.843ce0bffb5a7fe440de4413911645080840fd99: <reference osisRef="Ps.31.14-Ps.31.18">Psa 31:14-18</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_31:15-19) But, although a curse of the world and an offscouring of all people, he is confident in God, his Deliverer and Avenger. By ואני prominence is given to the subject by way of contrast, as in Psa 31:7. It appears as though Jahve had given him up in His anger; but he confides in Him, and in spite of this appearance, he even confides in Him with the prayer of appropriating faith. עתּות or אתּים (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.30">1Ch 29:30</reference>) are the appointed events and circumstances, the vicissitudes of human life; like the Arabic <hi type="italic">'idât</hi> (like עת from ועד), the appointed rewards and punishments. The times, with whatsoever they bring with them, are in the Lord’s hand, every lot is of His appointment or sending. The Vulgate follows the lxx, <hi type="italic">in manibus tuis sortes meae</hi>. The petitions of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">Psa 31:16</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.17">Psa 31:17</reference>, spring from this consciousness that the almighty and faithful hand of God has mould his life. There are three petitions; the middle one is an echo of the Aaronitish blessing in Num 6:25. כּי קראתיך, which gives the ground of his hope that he shall not be put to shame (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">Psa 31:2</reference>), is to be understood like אמרתּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.15">Psa 31:15</reference>, according to Ges. §126, 3. The expression of the ground for אל־אבושׁה, favours the explanation of it not so much as the language of petition (let me not be ashamed) of as hope. The futures which follow might be none the less regarded as optatives, but the order of the words does not require this. And we prefer to take them as expressing hope, so that the three petitions in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">Psa 31:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.17">Psa 31:17</reference>, correspond to the three hopes in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.18">Psa 31:18</reference>, Psa 31:19. He will not be ashamed, but the wicked shall be ashamed and silenced for ever. The form ידּמוּ, from דּמם, is, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.8.14">Jer 8:14</reference>, the plural of the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> ידּם, with the doubling of the first radical, which is customary in Aramaic (other examples of which we have in יקּד, ישּׁם, יתּם), not of the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. ידּם, the plural of which would be ידּמּוּ, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.9">1Sa 2:9</reference>; <hi type="italic">conticescere in orcum </hi>is equivalent to: to be silent, i.e., being made powerless to fall a prey to hades. It is only in accordance with the connection, that in this instance נאלם, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>, just like דּמם, denotes that which is forcibly laid upon them by the judicial intervention of God: all lying lips shall be dumb, i.e., made dumb. עתק prop. that which is unrestrained, free, insolent (cf. Arabic <hi type="italic">'âtik , 'atı̂k</hi>, unrestrained, free<note placement="foot">But these Arabic words do not pass over into the signification “insolent.”)</note> is the accusative of the object, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.4">Psa 94:4</reference>, and as it is the nominative of the subject in 1Sa 2:3.
entries.b6ce6713b1c7038d1acb4095536c7cd0da5ebd58: <reference osisRef="Ps.31.19-Ps.31.24">Psa 31:19-24</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_31:20-25) In this part well-grounded hope expands to triumphant certainty; and this breaks forth into grateful praise of the goodness of God to His own, and an exhortation to all to wait with steadfast faith on Jahve. The thought: how gracious hath Jahve been to me, takes a more universal form in Psa 31:20. It is an exclamation (מה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>) of adoring admiration. טוּב יהוה is the sum of the good which God has treasured up for the constant and ever increasing use and enjoyment of His saints. צפן is used in the same sense as in <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference>; cf. τὸ μάννα τὸ κεκρυμμένον, Rev 2:17. Instead of פּעלתּ it ought strictly to be נתתּ; for we can say פּעל טּוב, but not פּעל טוּב. What is meant is, the doing or manifesting of טּוב springing from this טוּב, which is the treasure of grace. Jahve thus makes Himself known to His saints for the confounding of their enemies and in defiance of all the world besides, Psa 23:5. He takes those who are His under His protection from the רכסי אישׁ, confederations of men (from רכס, Arab. <hi type="italic">rks , magna copia</hi>), from the wrangling, i.e., the slanderous scourging, of tongues. Elsewhere it is said, that God hides one in סתר אהלו (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>), or in סתר כּנפיו (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">Psa 61:5</reference>), or in His shadow (צל, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Psa 91:1</reference>); in this passage it is: in the defence and protection of His countenance, i.e., in the region of the unapproachable light that emanates from His presence. The סכּה is the safe and comfortable protection of the Almighty which spans over the persecuted one like an arbour or rich foliage. With בּרוּך ה David again passes over to his own personal experience. The unity of the Psalm requires us to refer the praise to the fact of the deliverance which is anticipated by faith. Jahve has shown him wondrous favour, inasmuch as He has given him a עיר מצור as a place of abode. מצור, from צוּר to shut in (Arabic <hi type="italic">misr</hi> with the denominative verb <hi type="italic">maṣṣara</hi>, to found a fortified city), signifies both a siege, i.e., a shutting in by siege-works, and a fortifying (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.60.11">Psa 60:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.108.11">Psa 108:11</reference>), i.e., a shutting in by fortified works against the attack of the enemy, 2Ch 8:5. The fenced city is mostly interpreted as God Himself and His powerful and gracious protection. We might then compare <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference> and other passages. But why may not an actual city be intended, viz., Ziklag? The fact, that after long and troublous days David there found a strong and sure resting-place, he here celebrates beforehand, and unconsciously prophetically, as a wondrous token of divine favour. To him Ziklag was indeed the turning-point between his degradation and exaltation. He had already said in his trepidation (חפז, <hi type="italic">trepidare</hi>), cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference> : I am cut away from the range of Thine eyes. נגרזתּי is explained according to גּרזן, an axe; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.54">Lam 3:54</reference>, נגרזתּי, and <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.5">Jon 2:5</reference>, נגרשׁתּי, favour this interpretation. He thought in his fear and despair, that God would never more care about him. אכן, <hi type="italic">verum enim vero</hi>, but Jahve heard the cry of his entreaty, when he cried unto Him (the same words as in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference>). On the ground of these experiences he calls upon all the godly to love the God who has done such gracious things, i.e., to love Love itself. On the one hand, He preserves the faithful (אמוּנים, from אמוּן = אמוּן, πιστοί, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>), who keep faith with Him, by also proving to them His faithfulness by protection in every danger; on the other hand, not scantily, but plentifully (על as in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.7">Isa 60:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jer 6:14</reference> : κατὰ περισσείαν) He rewardeth those that practise pride-in the sight of God, the Lord, the sin of sins. An animating appeal to the godly (metamorphosed out of the usual form of the expression חזק ואמץ, <hi type="italic">macte esto</hi>), resembling the animating call to his own heart in <reference osisRef="Ps.27.14">Psa 27:14</reference>, closes the Psalm. The godly and faithful are here called “those who wait upon Jahve.” They are to wait patiently, for this waiting has a glorious end; the bright, spring sun at length breaks through the dark, angry aspect of the heavens, and the <hi type="italic">esto mihi</hi> is changed into <hi type="italic">halleluja</hi>. This eye of hope patiently directed towards Jahve is the characteristic of the Old Testament faith. The substantial unity, however, of the Old Testament order of grace, or mercy, with that of the New Testament, is set before us in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>, which, in its New Testament and Pauline character, is the counterpart of <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1">Psa 19:1</reference>-14.  <chapter eID="Ps.31"/> <div eID="gen9364" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 31.
David, having been delivered from some great danger, or rather from many dangers, first relates the prayers which he had offered up to God amidst the terrors of death. He then subjoins his thanksgiving, which is no ordinary one; for he celebrates his deliverance at great length, and exhorts all the saints to be of good hope, as they had in him a most excellent and memorable example of God’s goodness.
To the chief musician. A psalm of David.
Psalm 31:1-4
1. In thee, O Jehovah! have I put my trust, let me not be ashamed for ever: deliver me in thy righteousness. 2. Incline thine ear unto me, deliver me speedily; be unto me a strong rock, a house of defense to save me. 3. For thou art my rock and my fortress: and for thy name’s sake thou wilt lead and guide me.
“Ou, adresse moy et conduy.” — Fr. marg. “Or, do thou direct and guide me.”
4. Pluck me out of the net which they have hidden for me; for thou art my strength.
 
1. In thee, O Jehovah! have I put my trust. Some are of opinion that this psalm was composed by David, after he had most unexpectedly escaped out of the wilderness of Maon; to which I do not object, although it is only a doubtful conjecture. Certainly he celebrates one or more of the greatest of his dangers. In the commencement he tells us what kind of prayer he offered in his agony and distress; and its language breathes affection of the most ardent nature. He takes it for a ground of hope that he trusted in the Lord, or continued to trust in him; for the verb in the past tense seems to denote a continued act. He held it as a principle, that the hope which depends upon God cannot possibly be disappointed. Meanwhile, we see how he brings forward nothing but faith alone; promising himself deliverance only because he is persuaded that he will be saved by the help and favor of God. But as this doctrine has been expounded already, and will yet occur oftener than once, it is sufficient at present to have glanced at it. Oh! that all of us would practice it in such a manner as that, whenever we approach to God, we may be able with David to declare that our prayers proceed from this source, namely, from a firm persuasion that our safety depends on the power of God. The particle signifying for ever may be explained in two ways. As God sometimes withdraws his favor, the meaning may not unsuitably be, Although I am now deprived of thy help, yet cast me not off utterly, or for evermore. Thus David, wishing to arm himself with patience against his temptations, would make a contrast between these two things, — being in distress for a time, and remaining in a state of confusion.
“Feroit une antithese entre ces deux choses, Estre en destresse pour un temps, et demeurer confus.” — Fr.
But if any one choose rather to understand his words in this way, “Whatever afflictions befall me, may God be ready to help me, and ever and anon stretch forth his hand to me, as the case requires,” I would not reject this meaning any more than the other. David desires to be delivered in the righteousness of God, because God displays his righteousness in performing his promise to his servants. It is too much refinement of reasoning to assert that David here betakes himself to the righteousness which God freely bestows on his people, because his own righteousness by works was of no avail. Still more out of place is the opinion of those who think that God preserves the saints according to his righteousness; that is to say, because having acted so meritoriously, justice requires that they should obtain their reward. It is easy to see from the frequent use of the term in The Psalms, that God’s righteousness means his faithfulness, in the exercise of which he defends all his people who commit themselves to his guardianship and protection. David, therefore, confirms his hope from the consideration of the nature of God, who cannot deny himself, and who always continues like himself.

                  <ns0:p n="8">8. And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Whereof I was in great and imminent Danger, if thou hadst not delivered me. See 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 23. 1.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="10">10. For my life <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="16">16. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal 4. 6.</ns0:note> Make thy face to shine upon thy ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Manifest thy Love and Favour to me, by answering my Prayers, and saving me from all mine Enemies.</ns0:note>: save me for thy mercies sake.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 25 2.</ns0:note> Let me not be ashamed, O LORD, for I have called upon thee <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And therefore thy Honour, will be Eclipsed in my Disap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointment, as if thou didst not hear Prayers, nor keep Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mise nor make any Difference between good and bad Men.</ns0:note>: let the wicked be ashamed <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Frustrated in their wicked Designs, and Carnal Confidences.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi>

                        </ns0:gap>ll.</ns0:note> grave <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Seeing they are implacable in their Malice and Rage, against innocent and good Men, do thou cut them off by thy just Judgment; and since either the Righteous, or the wicked must be cut off, let Destruction fall upon them, who most deserve it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> Let the lying lips <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Slanderous Tongues.</ns0:note> be put to silence <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either, by thy Vindication and discovery of my Integrity: Or, by some Eminent judgment, which may either Convince them, or cut them off.</ns0:note>, which speak <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a hard thing.</ns0:note> grievous things <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>hard Words,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Things,</ns0:hi> the singular Number, being put for the plural.                   <ns0:p n="19">19. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 64. 4. 1 Cor. 2. 9.</ns0:note> O how great <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy goodness <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">No words can express the greatness of thy Love and Bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sings.</ns0:note>, which thou hast laid up <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>hidden,</ns0:hi> to wit, with thy self, or in thy own Breast.
